beats.narration_text: People assume Claude is watching the Federal Register on its own. Wrong. It only tracks what a skill folder tells it to track. So — how does that folder actually track a filing deadline?

props.text:

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('know' -> 'track') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening on the regulator's side. A federal agency proposes a rule and opens a public comment period — often just sixty days before it can finalize. Miss that window and your objection never reaches the record. The easy assumption is that Claude is already watching that window, the way a person watches a calendar. It isn't. Claude has no built-in connection to any docket. What it has is a folder of instructions called comments — a skill. That distinction is the whole design choice: they gave you a plain-text procedure you can read, not a background service you have to trust.

shot.new_visual_element: An 'assumption' card ('CLAUDE IS WATCHING the docket, on its own') rings out and dims; two dim fact-chips slide past it, never touching

production_viz.label: No built-in connection to any docket
production_viz.mechanic: A card reads 'CLAUDE IS WATCHING / the docket, on its own', a terracotta ring pulses out from it and fades. The card dims. Two faint chips labelled 'comment period' and 'filing deadline' slide in from the side and pass beneath the assumption card without touching it. A caption fades in: 'no automatic connection to any docket.'

beats.narration_text: Open that folder and there's one file: SKILL.md. It says three things — review open comment periods, log decisions, track deadlines. That's the entire instruction set, in plain English. Claude reads it fresh every time and keeps no memory of a docket across sessions. They optimized for auditability at the expense of continuity — you can point at every line the model followed, but you also have to hand it the state each time. Watch one rule to see the machinery: a proposal opens its comment window on March second, sixty days to respond. The skill logs that date the moment it's told, and starts the clock.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- a SKILL.md card unfurls into three stacked instructions; a 'RULE OPENS · MAR 2' card beside a countdown ring filling toward 60 days

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- a rule opens, the clock starts
production_viz.mechanic: A card 'SKILL.md -- comments' splits into three stacked instruction lines: 'REVIEW OPEN PERIODS', 'LOG DECISIONS', 'TRACK DEADLINES'. Below, THE ANCHOR: a card 'RULE OPENS · MAR 2' beside a ring that fills from empty toward '60 DAYS' as the clock starts. THIS EXACT ANCHOR RETURNS, RESOLVED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Now the payoff. When day sixty arrives, the skill doesn't file anything itself — a person decides, and records that call with one flag: filed, not filed, or waived. For the March second rule, the log shows filed, on day fifty-nine. Notice what that flag does and doesn't buy you. A decision logged on time doesn't mean the comment itself was any good; the skill only kept the date, not the quality. And a rule with no logged decision isn't necessarily missed — it might be tracked in a spreadsheet the skill never saw. This works if you value a clean, auditable record of what you decided; it fails if you were hoping the calendar itself would tell you whether you did the right thing.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the countdown ring fills to day 59, a FILED stamp locks in; then splits into 'logged != good' and 'not logged != missed'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- logged on time, and only that
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 ANCHOR RETURNS -- the countdown ring for 'MAR 2 RULE' fills to 'DAY 59'; a 'FILED' stamp locks onto the log, terracotta-bordered highlight. It then splits into two cards: left reads 'filed, on time' beside a dimmed 'comment quality -- not tracked here' line, labelled 'logged != good'; right reads 'no logged decision' beside a separate 'tracked elsewhere?' card connected by a dashed line, labelled 'not logged != missed'.

beats.narration_text: So: the skill doesn't know the law, and it doesn't decide anything. It only remembers the date you gave it. Filed, waived, or missed — that call is still yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I want to file a public comment on a proposed federal rule, and I need to keep the deadline clean. The NPRM opens the comment period on some date and runs for sixty days. Walk me through what the comment period actually is and how the sixty-day clock is counted, which specific date my objection has to reach the record by, exactly what state you'd keep on my behalf about this rule — deadline, decision flag, evidence — and what you would not track, and how you'll ask me to record my decision as filed, not filed, or waived. Then ask me your first question. Go deeper: what changes when you're tracking dozens of open rules at once — where does a plain-text log break down, and what would you need before you'd trust the skill to be the only place a deadline lives?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to file a public comment on a proposed federal rule, and I need to keep the deadline clean. The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking says the comment period opens on [DATE] and runs for [N] days. Before we do anything else, walk me through: (1) what the comment period actually is and how the sixty-day clock is counted, (2) which specific date my objection has to be received by, (3) exactly what state you would keep on my behalf about this rule — deadline, decision flag, evidence — and what you would not track, and (4) how you will ask me to record my decision as filed, not filed, or waived. Then ask me your first question.
